title: DiScammer Defender: your local completion record
body_md:
## A record that lives in this browser

The checkpoints below read two things stored in this browser: the lessons you have marked complete and your result on the final self-assessment. To create a personal completion record, every lesson in all nine modules must be marked complete here, and the revised final self-assessment (2026-10-20) must have a saved result of **80% or higher**. An earlier pass is kept separately, but it does not count towards this current record. Type the name you want printed on it.

The record is made in your browser, for you. DiScammer does not issue, sign, proctor or validate it, and nobody watches you take the self-assessment, which you do at your own pace. If you explicitly switch on the optional progress sync, an encrypted bundle can carry your exam result and name; the server receives ciphertext, not a record it can read. Clear this browser’s data and the local copy may disappear. Open the site on another device and it will not be there unless you import or sync your progress. **Print / Save as PDF** gives you a personal copy of the record, and nothing more.

This record is **not a credential, verified or otherwise, and not an identity document.** It does not prove who you are, what you know or whether you could stop a real scam, and nobody has independently checked the score. A high score is a cue to keep practising, never permission to skip a check. One quirk of this exam revision: a passing result can survive a weaker retake, so look hard at the questions you just missed even when the checkpoint stays green.

## Write a plan of your own, and keep it private

Spend five minutes on a plan you will keep somewhere you control: a private note, or a sheet of paper. Leave account numbers, passwords, codes, real incident stories and financial details out of this lesson entirely.

1. **Pause trigger.** Write one sentence for the moment a message demands a sudden payment, a secret, a login or a change of account: “I will check this through a route I choose.” It gives you permission to interrupt someone else’s urgency.
2. **Independent contacts.** Save the real support route for your bank, taken from your card or banking app, plus one family contact and the workplace contact for payment or security questions. Note where each can be found, not the secrets that give access. Recheck them when they change.
3. **Account basics.** Start with your main email and your banking accounts. For each, check for a unique password or an available passkey, supported multi-factor sign-in (MFA), current recovery contacts and safe backup methods. A passkey strengthens a sign-in path where it is supported; it does not repair a weak recovery route.
4. **Payment rule.** For a new payee, a changed bank account or an unusual transfer, stop and confirm the exact recipient and purpose with a contact you already hold. If your organisation requires a second approver, get one. A real request can wait for the control.
5. **If something happened.** Note what was exposed: money, a password, a code, access to a device or identity data. Contact the relevant provider promptly, through its official route; ask for the remedy that suits the way you paid; secure the affected account; keep dates and reference numbers. Recovery is not guaranteed, and reporting routes vary by country.
6. **Practise with a person.** Tell one trusted person your callback rule, leaving out private details. Agree on a calm way to check a surprising request, even when the voice or video looks familiar. A code word can help but should never be the only check.

### Two questions before you print

Which two decisions in the exam or the simulation were hardest for you, and which independent route would you use in a real version of each? What would change if the request were genuine? If you have no answer yet, go back to those lessons and adjust the plan. What is worth having is a habit you carry out of this browser, not the look of the record.

**Sources and scope.** This plan draws on UK NCSC guidance on [verifying scam messages](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/phishing-scams/spot-scams) and [recovering an account](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/guidance/recovering-a-hacked-account), on NIST’s [distinctions between authenticators](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators/), and on US FTC [advice on what to do if you were scammed](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/what-do-if-you-were-scammed). All were checked on 2026-10-20. They support habits, not a DiScammer qualification. Your bank, your service, your employer and local law decide the real steps.
